(a) In General.—There are established within the Office, to carry out the programmatic responsibilities of the Office—
        (1) the Data Center; and 
        (2) the Research and Analysis Center.  
    (b) Data Center.—
        (1) General duties.—
            (A) Data collection.—The Data Center, on behalf of the Council, shall collect, validate, and maintain all data necessary to carry out the duties of the Data Center, as described in this subtitle. The data assembled shall be obtained from member agencies, commercial data providers, publicly available data sources, and financial entities under subparagraph (B). 
            (B) Authority.—
                (i) In general.—The Office may, as determined by the Council or by the Director in consultation with the Council, require the submission of periodic and other reports from any financial company for the purpose of assessing the extent to which a financial 
activity or financial market in which the financial company participates, or the financial company itself, poses a threat to the financial stability of the United States. 
                (ii) Mitigation of report burden.—Before requiring the submission of a report from any financial company that is regulated by a member agency, any primary financial regulatory agency, a foreign supervisory authority, or the Office shall coordinate with such agencies or authority, and shall, whenever possible, rely on information available from such agencies or authority. 
                (iii) Collection of financial transaction and position data.—The Office shall collect, on a schedule determined by the Director, in consultation with the Council, financial transaction data and position data from financial companies.  
            (C) Rulemaking.—The Office shall promulgate regulations pursuant to subsections (a)(1), (a)(2), (a)(7), and (c)(1) of section 153 regarding the type and scope of the data to be collected by the Data Center under this paragraph.  
        (2) Responsibilities.—
            (A) Publication.—The Data Center shall prepare and publish, in a manner that is easily accessible to the public—
                (i) a financial company reference database; 
                (ii) a financial instrument reference database; and 
                (iii) formats and standards for Office data, including standards for reporting financial transaction and position data to the Office.  
            (B) Confidentiality.—The Data Center shall not publish any confidential data under subparagraph (A).  
        (3) Information security.—The Director shall ensure that data collected and maintained by the Data Center are kept secure and protected against unauthorized disclosure. 
        (4) Catalog of financial entities and instruments.—The Data Center shall maintain a catalog of the financial entities and instruments reported to the Office. 
        (5) Availability to the council and member agencies.—The Data Center shall make data collected and maintained by the Data Center available to the Council and member agencies, as necessary to support their regulatory responsibilities. 
        (6) Other authority.—The Office shall, after consultation with the member agencies, provide certain data to financial industry participants and to the general public to increase market transparency and facilitate research on the financial system, to the extent that intellectual property rights are not violated, business confidential information is properly protected, and the sharing of such information poses no significant threats to the financial system of the United States.  
    (c) Research and Analysis Center.—
        (1) General duties.—The Research and Analysis Center, on behalf of the Council, shall develop and maintain independent analytical capabilities and computing resources—
            (A) to develop and maintain metrics and reporting systems for risks to the financial stability of the United States; 
            (B) to monitor, investigate, and report on changes in systemwide risk levels and patterns to the Council and Congress; 
            (C) to conduct, coordinate, and sponsor research to support and improve regulation of financial entities and markets; 
            (D) to evaluate and report on stress tests or other stability-related evaluations of financial entities overseen by the member agencies; 
            (E) to maintain expertise in such areas as may be necessary to support specific requests for advice and assistance from financial regulators; 
            (F) to investigate disruptions and failures in the financial markets, report findings, and make recommendations to the Council based on those findings; 
            (G) to conduct studies and provide advice on the impact of policies related to systemic risk; and 
            (H) to promote best practices for financial risk management.   
    (d) Reporting Responsibilities.—
        (1) Required reports.—Not later than 2 years after the date of enactment of this Act, and not later than 120 days after the end of each fiscal year thereafter, the Office shall prepare and submit a report to Congress. 
        (2) Content.—Each report required by this subsection shall assess the state of the United States financial system, including—
            (A) an analysis of any threats to the financial stability of the United States; 
            (B) the status of the efforts of the Office in meeting the mission of the Office; and 
            (C) key findings from the research and analysis of the financial system by the Office.

fable.w: The section requires the Office to promulgate regulations on the type and scope of data collected, and a rulemaking requirement counts as participation under the definition because it brings the public into the decision. The tempting reading is "No", since most of the consultation here is with the Council and member agencies and the reports go to Congress, all of which is inside the federal government. That reading fails because the rulemaking mandate independently satisfies the definition.
fable.s: The Office shall promulgate regulations pursuant to subsections (a)(1), (a)(2), (a)(7), and (c)(1) of section 153 regarding the type and scope of the data to be collected by the Data Center under this paragraph.

qwen_block.w: The section explicitly requires the Office to 'promulgate regulations'. The definition states that 'requiring rulemaking' is a form of participation. While much of the text involves internal coordination between federal agencies (which is not participation), the mandate to issue regulations triggers the 'Yes' label under the provided criteria.
qwen_block.s: (C) Rulemaking.—The Office shall promulgate regulations pursuant to subsections (a)(1), (a)(2), (a)(7), and (c)(1) of section 153 regarding the type and scope of the data to be collected by the Data Center under this paragraph.
qwen_block.b:
Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the section requires participation because it mentions "consultation with the Council" or "consultation with the member agencies." However, the Council and member agencies are federal entities (inside the government). The definition explicitly states that consultation between federal agencies or officials is not participation. Another potential trap is the mention of providing data to "financial industry participants and to the general public," but this is a one-way dissemination of information (publication/sharing), not a process where the public consults with or coordinates with the government *before* a decision is made. The rulemaking mentioned in (b)(1)(C) is a standard agency action, but without explicit mention of public comment periods or outside advisory boards in this specific text, it is less clear-cut than the other examples. However, looking closely at (b)(1)(B)(ii), it requires coordination with "foreign supervisory authority" before requiring reports. Foreign authorities are outside the US federal government. But is this "participation" in the sense of the definition? The definition says "consult or coordinate with people outside of the government... before making a decision." Requiring a report is a decision/action. Coordinating with a foreign authority is coordination with an outside entity. However, the primary actors are federal. Let's look for a stronger signal.

Actually, re-reading the definition: "Participation is when the federal government may or must consult or coordinate with people outside of the government before making a decision."
In (b)(1)(B)(ii): "Before requiring the submission of a report... the Office... shall coordinate with such agencies or authority [including foreign supervisory authority]". This is coordination with an outside entity (foreign authority) before a federal action (requiring a report). This fits the definition.

However, often "foreign supervisory authority" is treated similarly to other governments. Is a foreign government "outside the federal government"? Yes. The definition lists "state or local governments" as outside. It doesn't explicitly list foreign governments, but they are certainly not part of the US federal government.

Let's look for other instances.
(b)(1)(C) mentions rulemaking. Rulemaking generally implies public participation (comment periods), but the text doesn't explicitly say "public comment."
(b)(6) says "provide certain data to financial industry participants and to the general public". This is output, not input/participation in decision making.

Let's reconsider the "No" trap: "consultation or coordination BETWEEN federal agencies... is not participation."
(b)(1)(B)(ii) involves coordination with "member agency" (federal), "primary financial regulatory agency" (federal), "foreign supervisory authority" (non-federal), or "the Office" (federal). The coordination is with a mix. The requirement to coordinate with the foreign authority before requiring a report from a company regulated by that authority suggests a form of inter-agency/international coordination to avoid burden. Is this "participation"? The definition says "consult or coordinate with people outside of the government... before making a decision." The decision is "requiring the submission of a report." The coordination is with the foreign authority. This seems to fit.

However, in many legal contexts, coordination with foreign regulators is seen as administrative cooperation rather than "public participation" in the democratic sense (like hearings or advisory boards). But the definition is broad: "consult or coordinate with people outside of the government... These people might be state or local governments...". It doesn't exclude foreign governments.

Let's look at Example 9. It was "No" because the consultation was internal to the state/tribe plan submission, not with the federal agency on a federal decision. Here, the federal agency (Office) is making a decision (requiring a report) and must coordinate with an outside entity (foreign authority).

Is there a stronger "Yes"?
What about the "general public" in (b)(6)? "provide certain data... to the general public". This is not participation *by* the public in a decision. It's just access to information.

What about (c)(1)(B) "report... to Congress"? No, Congress is inside.

Let's look at the "Rulemaking" in (b)(1)(C). "The Office shall promulgate regulations...". Under the Administrative Procedure Act, rulemaking usually involves public comment. But the text itself doesn't explicitly mandate public comment. Example 6 labeled "Yes" for "may by regulation" because it gave authority to issue regulations. Here it says "shall promulgate regulations". This is a strong indicator of rulemaking, which is a form of participation (public comment). The definition says: "Answer 'Yes' when the SECTION involves ANY of the following: ... requiring rulemaking". This section *requires* rulemaking ("shall promulgate regulations"). Therefore, it is a Yes.

Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might focus on the internal consultations (with the Council, member agencies) and conclude "No" because they are intra-governmental. One might also dismiss the rulemaking clause as just an administrative task. However, the definition explicitly lists "requiring rulemaking" as a Yes.

Resolution: The section explicitly states "The Office shall promulgate regulations..." in subsection (b)(1)(C). The definition states that requiring rulemaking is a form of participation.

opus.w: The section requires the Office to make regulations on what data it collects, and the definition expressly treats a rulemaking requirement as participation. It also requires coordination with a foreign supervisory authority, which is outside the federal government, before the Office requires reports from financial companies. The tempting 'No' reading would rest only on the steps that stay inside the government (the Council, member agencies and reports to Congress), but it ignores the rulemaking requirement.
opus.s: (C) Rulemaking.—The Office shall promulgate regulations pursuant to subsections (a)(1), (a)(2), (a)(7), and (c)(1) of section 153 regarding the type and scope of the data to be collected by the Data Center under this paragraph.
opus.b: 1. **The tempting-but-wrong reading:** Most of the coordination here stays inside the federal government. The Office works with the Council, the Director and member agencies, and it reports to Congress. On that basis the answer would be "No." That reading misses subsection (b)(1)(C). It requires the Office to make regulations, and the definition counts a rulemaking requirement as participation. Separately, (b)(1)(B)(ii) requires coordination with "a foreign supervisory authority," which is outside the federal government. Both point to "Yes."

qwen_chat.w: The section describes the internal operations of a federal office (Data Center and Research and Analysis Center), including data collection from financial companies and reporting to Congress. While it mentions coordination with other agencies and consultation with the Council, these are all federal entities (inside the government). The interaction with financial companies is limited to data submission (reporting) and data publication (transparency), which does not constitute participation in a decision-making process as defined (e.g., consultation, advisory boards with outside members, public hearings).
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the requirement for the Office to "coordinate with such agencies or authority" (subsection (b)(1)(B)(ii)) or "consultation with the Council" constitutes participation. However, the "Council" and "member agencies" are federal entities (inside the government), and the coordination with "primary financial regulatory agency" or "foreign supervisory authority" is intra-governmental or international regulatory coordination, not public participation in a decision-making process as defined (which requires outside parties like the public, states, or non-federal entities to be consulted *before* a decision). The section primarily describes internal data collection, analysis, and reporting duties of a federal office. The only interaction with outside parties is the *collection* of data from financial companies (which is akin to an application/reporting requirement, not participation in a decision) and the *publication* of data to the public (which is transparency, not consultation/participation in a decision). There is no advisory board with outside members, no public comment period, no consultation with states/tribes/public before a decision, and no right to sue granted here.
